questions.stem: A visitor trips on a loose carpet seam in an architecture firm's reception area and breaks a wrist. Which of the firm's policies would typically respond to the visitor's claim?

options.text: Professional liability
options.explanation: Professional liability covers negligent professional services, such as design errors, not premises injuries.

options.text: Commercial general liability
options.explanation: Correct. CGL covers bodily injury and property damage arising from the firm's non-professional operations and premises.

options.text: Workers' compensation
options.explanation: Workers' comp covers the firm's own employees, not visitors.

options.text: Valuable papers
options.explanation: Valuable papers insurance covers loss of documents and records, not injuries.

questions.explanation: Match the loss to the policy: premises injury → CGL.

questions.stem: An architect retires and closes the firm. Its professional liability policy is claims-made. Two years later, a former client files a claim alleging a design error on a project completed while the policy was in force. What would have kept this claim covered?

options.text: Nothing. The policy covered the error because it was in force when the services were performed.
options.explanation: That describes occurrence-based coverage. Claims-made coverage responds to claims made while the policy (or a reporting extension) is in force.

options.text: An extended reporting period ("tail") endorsement bought when the policy ended
options.explanation: Correct. A tail extends the time to report claims arising from work performed before the policy ended.

options.text: An umbrella policy
options.explanation: Umbrella policies usually sit above CGL, auto and employer's liability. They don't extend professional liability reporting periods.

options.text: The client's builder's risk policy
options.explanation: Builder's risk covers physical loss to the work during construction, not claims against the architect.

questions.explanation: Claims-made policies need continuous coverage, or a tail, for claims that arrive after the policy ends.

questions.stem: A firm engages a renderer it calls an "independent contractor." Which facts suggest the renderer may legally be an employee?

options.text: The firm sets the renderer's daily hours and requires work in the office.
options.explanation: Correct. Control over when and where work is done points to employment.

options.text: The firm supplies the computer and software and trains the renderer in firm methods.
options.explanation: Correct. Supplying tools and training shows behavioral and financial control.

options.text: The renderer works only for this firm, full time, indefinitely.
options.explanation: Correct. Economic dependence on one firm with an ongoing relationship looks like employment.

options.text: The renderer invoices per project and markets services to other firms.
options.explanation: Per-project invoicing and serving other clients point toward independent-contractor status.

options.text: The written agreement labels the renderer an independent contractor.
options.explanation: Labels aren't controlling. The actual working relationship decides classification.

options.text: The renderer carries their own business insurance.
options.explanation: Carrying one's own business insurance points toward independence, not employment.

questions.explanation: Classification turns on control and economic reality, not on what the contract calls the person.

questions.stem: A non-exempt drafter works 46 hours one week at a regular rate of $30 per hour. Under the FLSA, what is the minimum gross pay for that week?

options.explanation: This is 46 × $30. It ignores the overtime premium on the 6 hours over 40.
This pays the 6 overtime hours at double time ($60), which the FLSA doesn't require.
This leaves out the 6 overtime hours entirely.

questions.explanation: Hours over 40 in a workweek → 1.5 × the regular rate for non-exempt employees.

questions.stem: An employee strains a back carrying sample boards to a client meeting. Which statement is generally correct?

options.text: Workers' compensation covers the injury regardless of fault and is generally the employee's exclusive remedy against the firm.
options.explanation: Correct. Workers' comp is a no-fault system and generally bars a separate negligence suit against the employer.

options.text: The employee must prove the firm was negligent to recover.
options.explanation: Workers' comp doesn't require proving employer negligence.

options.text: The firm's CGL policy covers the employee's medical bills.
options.explanation: CGL typically excludes injuries to the insured's own employees. Those go to workers' comp.

options.text: Coverage applies only if the injury happened in the office.
options.explanation: Work-related injuries away from the office, such as at a client meeting, are generally covered too.

questions.explanation: Employee injury → workers' compensation (no-fault, exclusive remedy).

questions.stem: Which statements about professional liability insurance for architects are generally true?

options.text: It is typically written on a claims-made basis.
options.explanation: Correct. Most architects' professional liability policies are claims-made.

options.text: Defense costs may reduce the available limit of liability.
options.explanation: Correct. Many policies have 'eroding' limits where defense spending reduces what remains for settlement.

options.text: It covers bodily injury to visitors at the firm's office.
options.explanation: Premises injuries fall under CGL, not professional liability.

options.text: It covers express warranties and guarantees the architect makes in a contract.
options.explanation: Policies generally exclude liability assumed by contract beyond the negligence standard, such as guarantees and warranties.

options.text: It is required by federal law for all architects.
options.explanation: No federal law requires it. Clients often require it by contract, and some jurisdictions have their own rules.

options.text: It pays to correct the contractor's defective workmanship.
options.explanation: Contractor workmanship is the contractor's responsibility, typically addressed through its warranty and insurance.

questions.explanation: Professional liability = negligence in professional services; claims-made; limits can erode; contractual guarantees excluded.

questions.stem: A 30-person firm has a project manager who needs eight weeks off to care for a parent with a serious health condition. The manager has worked there three years full time. What does federal law generally require?

options.text: Nothing, because the firm has fewer than 50 employees.
options.explanation: Correct. The FMLA applies to employers with 50 or more employees, so federal law doesn't require this leave. State law or firm policy may still provide it.

options.text: Up to 12 weeks of paid leave under the FMLA
options.explanation: FMLA leave is unpaid. The FMLA also doesn't reach a 30-person employer.

options.text: Up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave under the FMLA
options.explanation: This describes the FMLA's benefit, but it applies only to employers with 50+ employees.

options.text: Leave only if the employee is exempt.
options.explanation: Exempt status under the FLSA has nothing to do with family leave eligibility.

questions.explanation: The FMLA covers employers with 50 or more employees (29 U.S.C. §2611(4)). Many states have their own family-leave laws covering smaller employers, so check the state; the ARE tests the federal concept. Know the thresholds: FMLA 50+, COBRA 20+, ADEA 20+, Title VII and ADA 15+.

questions.stem: An architect sends a junior designer to document existing conditions at an occupied renovation site where demolition is underway. What is the firm's most appropriate action?

options.text: Provide appropriate PPE and site-safety training, and have the designer follow the contractor's site safety rules.
options.explanation: Correct. The firm has an employer duty to protect its own staff, while the contractor stays responsible for overall jobsite safety.

options.text: Take over the contractor's site safety program while the designer is on site.
options.explanation: Taking control of site safety moves the contractor's responsibility onto the architect. Architects should avoid this.

options.text: No action is needed, because jobsite safety is the contractor's sole responsibility.
options.explanation: The contractor controls the jobsite, but the firm still has OSHA employer duties toward its own employees.

options.text: Require the client to sign a waiver of the designer's injuries.
options.explanation: A client can't waive an employee's workers' comp rights, and a waiver doesn't fix a safety obligation.

questions.explanation: Protect your own staff without assuming the contractor's site-safety role.

questions.stem: A firm switches professional liability carriers. What should it make sure the new policy includes?

options.text: A retroactive date matching the original policy, so prior acts stay covered
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the original retro date (prior-acts coverage) means claims about earlier work are still covered under the new claims-made policy.

options.text: A retroactive date equal to the new policy's start date
options.explanation: That would leave all earlier work uninsured for claims made in the future.

options.text: Occurrence-based professional liability coverage
options.explanation: Occurrence-based professional liability is rarely available to architects. The practical fix is continuous claims-made coverage.

options.text: A higher deductible to reduce premium
options.explanation: A deductible choice doesn't address the coverage gap for earlier work.

questions.explanation: With claims-made coverage, continuity of the retroactive date is what protects prior work.

questions.stem: An employee uses a personal car to drive to a site visit and causes an accident that injures another driver. Which coverages are most likely to respond?

options.text: The employee's personal auto policy
options.explanation: Correct. The owner's personal auto policy is typically primary for that vehicle.

options.text: The firm's hired and non-owned auto coverage
options.explanation: Correct. Non-owned auto coverage protects the firm when employees use their own vehicles on firm business.

options.text: The firm's professional liability policy
options.explanation: Driving isn't a professional design service. Professional liability won't respond.

options.text: The firm's workers' compensation policy, for the other driver's injuries
options.explanation: Workers' comp covers the firm's employees, not third parties injured in an accident.

options.text: The project owner's builder's risk policy
options.explanation: Builder's risk covers physical loss to the work under construction.

options.text: The firm's valuable papers policy
options.explanation: Valuable papers covers loss of records, not auto liability.

questions.explanation: Employee-owned vehicles on firm business are a common gap. Hired and non-owned auto coverage fills it.

flashcards.back: Claims alleging negligent acts, errors or omissions in professional services. Usually claims-made; may have eroding limits.
Bodily injury and property damage from non-professional operations or premises. Usually occurrence-based. Excludes professional services.
The policy in force when the claim is made responds, as long as the act happened after the retroactive date.
The policy in force when the injury or damage occurred responds, even if the claim comes years later.
Extended reporting period bought when a claims-made policy ends (retirement or closure) for later claims about past work.
Keeping the original retroactive date when switching carriers so earlier work stays insured.
State-mandated, no-fault coverage for employee work injuries; generally the employee's exclusive remedy against the employer.
Non-exempt employees: 1.5× regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek.

flashcards.front: What makes an employee exempt from overtime
flashcards.back: Both a duties test (e.g., learned professional) and salary basis at no less than $684/week (29 C.F.R. §541.600). Title alone doesn't count.

flashcards.front: Employee vs. independent contractor: deciding factor
flashcards.back: Control (behavioral, financial) and economic dependence, not the contract label.
Title VII & ADA: 15+. ADEA & COBRA: 20+. FMLA & ACA mandate: 50+. (States often cover smaller employers.)
Protects the firm when employees use personal or rented vehicles on firm business.
Employment practices liability: discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination claims.

flashcards.front: Who is responsible for jobsite safety?
flashcards.back: The contractor (A201-2017 §3.3.1, Art. 10). The architect protects its own staff but shouldn't take control of site safety.
Employers with 20+ employees; coverage generally 18 months after a qualifying event; the employee can be charged up to 102% of the premium.
